articles.summary: A Diwali celebration in Seattle was disrupted on Saturday (local time) after far-right American activist Jake Lang and a group of protesters attempted to
articles.body: A Diwali celebration in Seattle was disrupted on Saturday (local time) after far-right American activist Jake Lang and a group of protesters attempted to interrupt the festivities while carrying placards reading "Deport All Dot Heads". Lang was confronted and physically stopped by some of the people present at the event.Following the incident, Lang posted pictures of the attempted disruption on X and launched an abusive tirade against Hindus, accusing them of being responsible for turning Texas blue in favour of the Democrats.US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal and other prominent Indian Americans have condemned the disruption.In a post on X, Jayapal expressed outrage over the incident, describing it as a racist display and saying the Indian-American community should be able to celebrate the festival without fear."I am beyond disgusted by this vile and racist display. Diwali is an important holiday and our community should feel safe to celebrate it. This hateful display has no place in our city or this country," she wrote.Indian-American businessman Ajay Jain Bhutoria also condemned the incident, calling it "pure bigotry" and saying racial slurs targeting Hindus had no place in the United States."Absolutely disgusting. Jake Lang and Thomas Allen storming a peaceful Diwali celebration in Seattle with signs reading “Deport All Dot Heads” and “Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians” is pure hate and bigotry. Diwali is a festival of light, family, and joy — not a threat. Targeting Hindu Americans and Indian immigrants with racial slurs and conspiracy rhetoric has no place in this country. We stand against this racism and for the right of every American to celebrate their heritage freely. #StopAsianHate," he said in a post on X.The Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA) also condemned the disruption and urged community members in Seattle and surrounding areas to remain vigilant, warning that the activists had announced plans to disrupt other Diwali celebrations.In a post on X, the organisation said, "Community Alert for Seattle and surrounding areas! Hinduphobic bigotry on open display as activists Jake Lang and Thomas Allen burst in to disrupt a Hindu Diwali celebration where children are performing, holding signs such as “Deport all Dotheads” and “Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians”. Thankfully, there were others who didn’t tolerate this and removed them from the premises. We condemn such actions and advise community members to stay vigilant while celebrating Diwali, as these activists have announced plans to disrupt other celebrations."Lang heads an organisation called White Replacement and was among those who participated in the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol. He served four years in prison before being pardoned by US President Donald Trump on the first day of his second presidency in 2025.The incident came shortly after Trump celebrated Diwali at the White House with Indian tech entrepreneur Vishal Gondal, chef Vikas Mehta and others at the Oval Office. The US President participated in a ceremonial diya-lighting and was presented with a copy of the Hanuman Chalisa.Meanwhile, Washington State Governor Bob Ferguson also marked the festival at the state's Legislative Building in Olympia, alongside the Consul General of India and state Senator Manka Dhingra.In a post on X, Ferguson said, "We had an incredible celebration of Diwali inside the Legislative Building this week with the Consulate General of India and Sen. Dhingra, and I proclaimed this Sunday to be Diwali, The Festival of Lights In Washington State. Washington state is proud to be home to one of the largest communities of Indian Americans in the country. During the previous decade, we had the fastest growing Indian American population in the entire country. And we have seen this community contribute so much to our state."The attempted disruption in Seattle also comes days after another right-wing activist allegedly plotted a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago. A 19-year-old suspect, identified as Alexandros Paporakis, was arrested following an investigation into threats against the temple. The suspect, who professed Nazi ideology, had allegedly outlined a plan to carry out an attack.Meanwhile, Lang has also claimed that the US midterm election results, which saw Democrats make gains in states such as Texas and Kansas, were rigged. Calling for a protest ahead of the anniversary of the January 6 Capitol attack, he said, "On January 3rd 2027, Christian Crusaders will descend upon the US Capitol in Washington DC to PROTEST the Certification of the RIGGED Midterms!!!!"Texas saw Democratic victories in the Senate and gubernatorial races, with James Talarico winning the Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa becoming governor.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1883, Harriet Strong was left with four daughters and a debt-ridden ranch after her husband’s death; she later developed water-storage systems that anticipated major US projects
articles.summary: In 1883, Harriet Williams Russell Strong found herself responsible for a struggling California ranch, four young daughters and debts left behind by her
articles.body: In 1883, Harriet Williams Russell Strong found herself responsible for a struggling California ranch, four young daughters and debts left behind by her late husband. She had little experience managing agricultural land and was still dealing with persistent health problems. The ranch, however, depended on something she soon began to understand better than most experienced farmers: water. As she worked to keep the property financially viable, Strong developed ways to store and control water for irrigation, eventually securing several US patents. Her work took her beyond farming and into public policy, where she argued for large-scale water management projects that would influence the development of the American West.How Harriet Strong inherited a debt-ridden ranch in 1883Harriet Strong's circumstances changed dramatically in 1883 when her husband, Charles Strong, died by suicide following the collapse of another business venture. He had lost money in a mining investment that turned out to be worthless, leaving Harriet to deal with the financial consequences. At the time, she was in Philadelphia receiving treatment for a longstanding spinal condition. Her four daughters, aged between 10 and 14, were living in Whittier, California.According to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), after completing her treatment, Harriet returned to California and took responsibility for the family's 220-acre Rancho del Fuerte. The property was facing financial difficulties, and creditors were seeking to recover the money owed by her late husband. She had no formal agricultural training and was not in particularly good health, but losing the ranch was not an option she was prepared to accept.She began studying farming through books, scientific publications and conversations with neighbouring landowners. Her research covered everything from soil conditions and crop selection to irrigation and agricultural markets.How walnut farming and pampas grass helped her rebuild the businessStrong identified walnuts as a potentially profitable crop and devoted around 150 acres of the property to growing walnut trees. There was a practical difficulty, though. The trees needed substantial quantities of water and took years to produce a commercial harvest. She needed another source of income while waiting for the orchard to mature.As reported by USPTO), her solution was Argentine pampas grass, a fast-growing plant that could be cultivated between the rows of walnut trees. Its decorative plumes were increasingly popular during the Victorian period, particularly as alternatives to feathers used in fashionable hats. Strong recognised that the crop could provide an additional income stream without requiring her to abandon the long-term walnut plan.Pampas plumes sold wholesale for around four cents each, a considerable sum for the period, and Strong found ways to keep the business going as consumer tastes changed. She supplied coloured red, white and blue plumes for the 1892 and 1896 Democratic and Republican national conventions, turning the decorative grass into a product with a market beyond ordinary household and fashion use.How a walnut orchard inspired Harriet Strong's water inventionsThe success of the walnut orchard depended heavily on reliable irrigation. Southern California's climate presented a difficult combination of limited rainfall and sudden, destructive floods. Heavy storms could send large volumes of water through the Los Angeles basin, damaging farmland and carrying away resources that might otherwise have been stored for dry periods.Strong began working on ways to address both problems. Instead of allowing stormwater to run off the land, she developed a system of reservoirs and interconnected dams designed to retain water for agricultural use. Her approach involved a series of ascending dams, with each structure helping to support the one above it.Beginning in 1887, Strong secured patents covering dam and reservoir construction and irrigation systems. She eventually became the named inventor on five US patents.The 1893 Chicago World's Fair brought wider recognitionStrong's business success gave her an opportunity to present her agricultural and inventive work to a national audience. At the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, she received two medals for her inventions and promoted the products grown on her ranch.One of the most unusual displays associated with her visit was the Pampas Plume Palace, an elaborate structure made largely from the grass she cultivated. Her daughters helped with its construction. The display attracted attention at a time when decorative pampas plumes were a fashionable commercial product.The fair also gave Strong a platform to discuss women's participation in business. She spoke at a congress devoted to business training for women, arguing that practical knowledge of commercial affairs could help women take a greater role in public administration.How Harriet Strong expanded her work beyond agricultureBy the early 20th century, Strong's interests had expanded well beyond her ranch. Her knowledge of water management brought her into discussions about flood prevention and the infrastructure needed to support agriculture across Southern California.She played a part in the campaign that led to the Los Angeles Flood Control Act of 1915 and served on a flood control board. Her public involvement came at a time when women in the United States were still fighting for basic political representation. California had granted women the right to vote in 1911, but Strong's participation in public affairs had begun before that change.In 1918, she became the first woman delegate to attend a convention of the US Chamber of Commerce, another indication of how far her career had moved from the management of a single agricultural property.Her Colorado River proposal reached Congress during World War IDuring the First World War, Strong travelled to Washington, DC, to present Congress with a proposal for a major dam on the Colorado River, near the lower end of the Grand Canyon. Her plan was intended to achieve several objectives at once: regulate flooding, conserve water, generate hydroelectric power and provide irrigation to farmland.The agricultural argument was particularly relevant during wartime. Strong believed that a dependable water supply could increase food production in the American West, helping the United States support Allied forces and civilians affected by the conflict.She viewed the Colorado River as a resource that needed to be managed on a regional scale rather than through isolated agricultural projects. Her proposal anticipated the role that large dams and canal networks would later play in supplying water to farms and settlements across the region.Congress did not approve her plan as the war came to an end. Strong believed the proposal had been dismissed partly because it had come from a woman rather than because of its practical merits.Hoover Dam and the All-American Canal followed years laterHarriet Strong died in a car accident in 1926, before the large Colorado River projects she had advocated for became reality. Her ideas, however, remained relevant as the federal government moved towards developing major water infrastructure in the region.Congress approved the Boulder Canyon Project in 1928, providing the legislative foundation for the construction of Hoover Dam. Work on the structure was completed in 1935. The dam became a major source of hydroelectric power while helping regulate the Colorado River and store water for use across the Southwest.The legislation also provided for the All-American Canal, a major irrigation project intended to carry Colorado River water into California's Imperial Valley. Construction began in 1942, and the canal became a central part of the region's agricultural water supply.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: No engineers, no workshop: 17-year-old Gurugram student builds Rs 1 lakh solar vehicle that could make everyday travel cheaper, running at just 13 paise per km
articles.summary: What can a school student do with some knowledge of mathematics, an interest in automobiles and a problem he wants to solve?
articles.body: What can a school student do with some knowledge of mathematics, an interest in automobiles and a problem he wants to solve? For 17-year-old Akshit Khera from Gurugram, the answer was a working solar-assisted three-wheeler that could help make everyday transport more affordable for families.The Class 12 student designed and built the vehicle at a final cost of Rs 102,536, with an estimated running cost of 13 paise per kilometre. As reported by India Today, Akshit developed the prototype with a weatherproof two-seat cabin, a cargo box and a 400W solar panel that also serves as a roof. The project was driven by a simple concern: how can people who depend on local transport afford a vehicle of their own? Akshit summed up his approach by saying, "I didn't have a workshop, a team of engineers or a big budget. I had a question, some school maths and physics, and a lot of curiosity."A conversation at home gave him the ideaThe project did not begin with a school assignment or a competition. It started after Akshit spoke to his housemaid's family, who had moved to Gurugram and were finding local transportation expensive. The man in the family worked as a driver and transported cargo. When Akshit asked why he did not buy a vehicle and start a small business of his own, he learnt that the purchase price and running expenses made it difficult.Electric loaders were an option, but their prices, estimated at Rs 1.5 lakh to Rs 2 lakh, were still too high for the family. Akshit then spoke to around 20 other families and found that the need for an affordable vehicle was not limited to one household. "I spoke to about 20 more families, and it became clear that there was a real need for an affordable, low-running-cost vehicle that could serve different purposes," he said. He wanted to build something that could carry goods as well as passengers. His first thought was to make a completely solar-powered vehicle. But after studying sunlight availability across seasons and calculating the distance it needed to travel, he realised that relying only on solar energy would not be practical. He therefore chose a solar-assisted design.How the solar three-wheeler worksThe vehicle can cover at least 50 km on a single charge, with the solar panel providing additional energy during the day. Its design includes seating for two and a cargo box, with a stated carrying capacity of up to 300 kg. The 400W solar panel has two purposes. It generates electricity to support the vehicle and also works as a protective canopy over the cargo area.According to Akshit's calculations, solar energy can meet around 63 per cent of the electricity needed for an average daily run of 50 km. This contribution is expected to change with the seasons. His estimates put it at around 41 per cent during the monsoon and up to 87 per cent in peak summer. The 13-paise running cost is also an estimate based on these calculations, not a figure established through extensive real-world testing. Akshit says the vehicle uses around 2.46 kWh of energy to cover 50 km. With the estimated solar contribution taken into account, the remaining electricity cost works out to approximately 13 paise per kilometre.From a Rs 1.35 lakh estimate to a Rs 1 lakh buildKeeping the cost under control was one of the biggest parts of the project. The initial estimate was around Rs 1.35 lakh, but Akshit reviewed the design and components to bring the final cost down to Rs 1,02,536. He reduced the battery requirement from 5.38 kWh to 3.072 kWh and used heavier steel tubes only at important load-bearing points. This helped reduce the vehicle's weight by 26 kg and save around Rs 2,100. He also visited Delhi's Mayapuri automobile market, compared quotations from different vendors and negotiated component prices. These efforts helped him save more than Rs 17,000.The project also required several practical decisions. Akshit chose a lithium-ion battery over a lead-acid alternative, considering its longer lifespan. He selected painted steel sheets for the cargo box floor instead of plywood, which could swell or deteriorate after repeated exposure to rain.Finding someone to fabricate the vehicle was another challenge. More than a dozen workshops across Gurugram, Delhi and Faridabad turned down the project before a fabricator named Arun agreed to help. Akshit also had to redesign the charging system after the solar panel's voltage requirements made his original controller choice unsuitable. Reflecting on the experience, he said, "The biggest lesson for me was that every setback was cheaper to fix on paper than in reality."A prototype today, a bigger plan for tomorrowAkshit's interest in vehicle design had already taken him beyond the classroom. In 2025, he worked as the lead design and manufacturing engineer for Apex Racing at the STEM Racing World Finals in Singapore. The team competed against 82 others and recorded the seventh-fastest average time. His parents, Amit Khera and Kanchan Khera, supported him through the calculations, vendor visits and fabrication process. Their support helped him take the idea from paper to a working prototype.However, Akshit does not consider the three-wheeler a finished commercial product yet. It has undergone only initial testing, and he wants to evaluate its performance under different sunlight and weather conditions before making stronger claims about its efficiency. He estimates that large-scale manufacturing could reduce the cost by 10 to 20 per cent. He hopes to work with an automobile manufacturer on safety checks, durability testing, certification and a service network, while keeping affordability at the centre of the design.He has also committed to donating the vehicle to a family in need. For now, his next steps include exploring lighter solar cells, better materials, swappable batteries and shared solar-charging points. His project is a reminder that innovation does not always begin with expensive equipment or a professional team. Sometimes, it starts with noticing a problem around you and being curious enough to try solving it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Russia may have lost up to 450,000 in Ukraine war, leaked death records claim
articles.summary: Between 394,000 and 450,000 people fighting on Russia's side or otherwise linked to the war in Ukraine may have died since the start of Moscow's
articles.body: Between 394,000 and 450,000 people fighting on Russia's side or otherwise linked to the war in Ukraine may have died since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to death records allegedly obtained from Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) by two hacker groups.Belarusian Cyberpartisans and Silent Crow, which claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Rosstat, published the estimates on November 7, saying they had accessed the agency's internal Demography database containing information from death certificates registered between February 2022 and August 2026.Belarusian Cyberpartisans estimated at least 393,881 deaths based on records that explicitly identified military operations as the cause. Silent Crow put the figure at up to 450,100, using a broader methodology that also included non-combat deaths of military personnel and certain deaths recorded without a specified cause.The Kyiv Independent said it could not immediately verify the authenticity of the leaked records or the casualty estimates.According to estimates based on data from the Ukrainian open-source mapping project DeepState, Russia has gained control of approximately 73,000 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory since launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Comparing this with Silent Crow's estimate of 450,100 deaths would amount to roughly six deaths for every square kilometre of territory seized, although the casualty figures have not been independently verified.The hackers said they had gained access to Rosstat's network around six months before launching the attack, systematically collecting internal documents and other data before targeting the agency's IT infrastructure overnight between October 31 and November 1.Rosstat acknowledged that its systems had been targeted in cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1 but denied that its databases had been compromised or information leaked. The agency later reported disruptions to some of its services and extended deadlines for submitting certain statistical data.Russia does not disclose its military casualties in Ukraine, making independent assessments of the death toll difficult.As of November 6, independent Russian outlet Mediazona, working with BBC Russian and volunteers, had identified 285,881 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine through open-source research. The journalists have repeatedly stressed that their verified count is incomplete and that the actual death toll is considerably higher.The casualty estimates come ahead of another round of negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the United States, scheduled to take place on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, as efforts continue to find a way to end the war.The talks would be the fourth round of negotiations brokered by the Trump administration, with the most recent meeting held in Geneva in February.Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the deadlock, although key issues concerning territory and security remain unresolved.You use AI every day. articles.title: Archaeologists discover rare gold bear ornament in ancient Saka burial mound in Kazakhstan, alongside human remains and scattered artefacts
articles.summary: Archaeologists have discovered what appears to be a gold bear figurine at a Saka-period burial mound in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
articles.body: Archaeologists have discovered what appears to be a gold bear figurine at a Saka-period burial mound in Almaty, Kazakhstan. The find was made during emergency excavations at the Karagaily burial ground in the Nauryzbay district. The mound had been looted in ancient times, leaving artefacts scattered across the site. The burial mound is provisionally dated to the 4th-3rd centuries BCE.According to the Almaty city administration, the ornament is believed to be a small cast-gold bear intended to decorate a headdress. Archaeologists also recovered numerous human remains and fragments of Saka pottery. Researchers believe four adults and three children may have been buried there, although the exact number is not yet known.The rare gold bear figurine and its connection to Saka headdressesThe most notable find appears to be a small gold figurine shaped like a bear. Archaeologists believe it was made by casting and may have been used to decorate a headdress. Holes in the plate suggest that the ornament could have been sewn onto the headwear.The Almaty city administration said similar objects were characteristic of Saka-period clothing. It cited a gold finial shaped like an argali found on the headdress of the Golden Man. Another comparison came from the Kok-Kainar burial ground, where a small leopard sculpture was found in 2014. That object was also an element of a headdress. The bear figurine is described by the museum association’s director as unique to Kazakhstan, with no similar find previously recorded there.What archaeologists found inside the ancient Saka burial moundThe Karagaily burial mound measures 25-26 metres in diameter and about 2.5 metres high. A preliminary dating based on study of the burial ground places it in the Saka period, between the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. The mound had been looted in ancient times, and the looting pit measures three metres.Excavations uncovered a significant quantity of human remains, as well as fragments of Saka pottery. Most of the artefacts had been scattered after the looting. Researchers believe the mound may have contained the burials of four adults and three children. However, the exact number of people buried there has not yet been established. Further analysis is planned to clarify the burial circumstances and establish the number of individuals.What makes the ancient gold bear ornament significantMarat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior researcher at the Almaty Museum Association, said the unusually large number of remains recovered there was of particular interest. Such burials are uncommon in Kazakhstan, he added.Burial mounds of a similar size were generally intended for one or two people. Researchers plan to carry out additional analyses to clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals. The work will include specialists in anthropology.Lyazzat Kudaibergenovna Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museum Association, said, "The sculptural bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered before. This discovery makes it possible to trace cultural parallels across the entire Eurasian region, from the Black Sea region to the Altai.”Other archaeological discoveries across AlmatyAfter the archaeological investigations and scientific processing of the recovered materials are complete, the most valuable artefacts are expected to be included in an exhibition at the Almaty Museum and shown to the public. The Almaty Museum Association received a special licence for archaeological excavations in 2022 and began conducting independent research in the city.That year, it found an undisturbed Saka warrior burial in the Alatau district, dating from the 5th to 2nd centuries BCE. Finds included fragments of a gold-inlaid sword, gold animal-style ornaments, silver objects, and human remains. In 2024, excavations found human bones, bronze fasteners, and nails. In 2025, archaeologists identified an ancient looters’ tunnel in one mound.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Hertfordshire couple used an inherited Chinese brush pot as a doorstop for 40 years; experts identified the late 18th- or early 19th-century carving, which sold for a £150,000 hammer price
articles.summary: A valuable 18th-century Chinese brush pot, originally used as a doorstop in a Hertfordshire cottage for four decades, sells for £150,000 at auction after being recognized for its artistic and cultural significance. Discover the story of hidden heritage and expert appraisal in the world of antiques.
articles.body: A Chinese antique worth £250,000 spent 40 years doing an everyday household chore in a Hertfordshire cottage. Its owners, who inherited it, used it as a doorstop, not knowing the carved wooden ornament was a valuable example of traditional Chinese craftsmanship. The auctioneer, called in to value the family's other possessions, recognised the object as a calligrapher's brush pot carved from zitan wood and decorated with the Hundred Boys motif, dating to the late 18th or early 19th century. Antiques Trade Gazette reported it sold at Sworders' Asian art sale in May 2014.An overlooked object comes to lightThe pair inherited the brush pot and kept it at their home for nearly 40 years. They propped it in the doorway to a sitting room as a doorstop. Its importance was realised when an auctioneer visited to assess the rest of the cottage's contents. The brush pot intrigued Richard Harrison, who recognised it as an 18th-century Chinese carving, which was to become a major feature of an Asian art sale.It was a carved Zitan wood ‘Hundred Boys’ biotong, or brush pot, by Sworders, measuring approximately 2.45 cm high; it was dated to the late 18th/early 19th century. It was hammered at £150,000 in April 2014. It was a “famous and important” lot which Sworders believed would have excellent prospects. There were dozens of small boys carved into the lively design, and a report of the sale quoted Harrison as describing the figure as 'almost three-dimensional' and 'doing all sorts of things,' notably 'setting off firecrackers'. He also commented on the remarkable condition of the object, which had been used for many years as a doorstop.The craft and meaning behind a Chinese brush A bitong is the Chinese term for a brush pot. They were placed on the desk alongside writers' or painters' brushes and tools. They served an everyday utilitarian function but also displayed dexterity and art. Unlike the other writing instruments kept in the scholar's studio, the brush pot was the vessel that was merely functional. The tools of writing and painting defined the scholar's studio, where brushes and ink stones were kept, and the owner's taste was displayed. The barrel-shaped vessel was carved with an inviting little scene to be examined up close: the Hundred Boys motif symbolised good luck and prosperity for offspring. Carved brush pots were made from many materials, from bamboo and wood, but Chinese furniture makers and carvers especially prized zitan as it was a dense, very desirable timber with tightly grained and dark coloured.Academic research helps explain why these objects deserve attention beyond their practical purpose. A study in Arte Individuo y Sociedad examines Chinese curved bamboo stationery, connecting decorative models with painting and literacy culture research published in Trans/ Form/ Acao, brings together the carved brush pot and closely examines the Hertfordshire example to show how the carved brush conveyed the language of a spatialisation found in landscape painting in three dimensions. The piece is carved from Zitan wood rather than bamboo, but these studies give insight into the artistic aspiration of a scholar's object.A £150,000 reminder of hidden heritageThe sale also reinforces how valuable expert knowledge is when it comes to spotting antiques. Without the visit, the pot would have been just a hard-to-ship paperweight. Sworders, based in Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, established a specialist Asian art department and drew in collectors from markets such as Hong Kong and Mainland China, and the auction house later described the brush pot as one of the leading Chinese art sales.£150,000 was the hammer price, not what was paid after the premium. To the couple, The Hunt started as part of a normal valuation of household contents and finished as the realisation that an heirloom had travelled through one of the most prominent artistic circles in the world.You use AI every day. articles.title: Military cadet, far-right obsession: What we know about 25-year-old Poland shooter
articles.summary: A 25-year-old man believed to be a military school cadet, who neighbours described as a quiet and polite individual, has been identified as the suspect
articles.body: A 25-year-old man believed to be a military school cadet, who neighbours described as a quiet and polite individual, has been identified as the suspect behind a deadly shooting in Poland's historic city of Krakow. Dressed in military-style fatigues and armed with an assault rifle, the gunman allegedly drove through the city's busy Main Market Square on Saturday, opening fire at pedestrians and other targets.The attack left six people dead, including a British national, and 15 others injured. Police eventually shot and wounded the suspect, who was taken to hospital for treatment. Polish authorities have described the incident as an act of terror, with the country's interior minister saying preliminary findings point to the man's fascination with far-right ideologies and his ultranationalistic views.Military cadet with far-right viewsAccording to the Daily Mail, the suspect was dressed in military-style fatigues when he drove a black Subaru into Krakow's Main Market Square at around 3pm local time. He allegedly opened fire using an AR-15-style assault rifle, targeting a tram, pedestrians and two horses.The Independent reported that the 25-year-old drove to multiple locations within the square, firing an automatic weapon at each stop. He was also wearing a bulletproof vest, according to Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cislo. Police subsequently found additional weapons and ammunition inside his vehicle.Although authorities have not officially released his identity, interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said the suspect held 'very radical' and 'ultranationalistic' views."Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwinski said at a news conference.Neighbours, however, described the suspect as an unremarkable and quiet individual, saying they had not noticed anything suspicious about his behaviour."A polite, quiet guy. We can't say anything bad about him," residents of his apartment building told Polish media, according to the Daily Mail.Family members found dead at homeIn another development, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had discovered the bodies of three people, two women and a man, at the suspect's family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, around 150km north-east of Krakow.The victims are believed to be the suspect's close family members. However, authorities have not publicly established the circumstances surrounding their deaths.Meanwhile, footage from the shooting showed a police officer approaching the suspect, who was lying on the road, and firing several shots at close range. The officer, who had reportedly already been hit three times, subsequently collapsed after being seriously wounded.Two police officers were seriously injured in the incident, with both remaining in critical condition, according to the Daily Mail. The suspect also sustained injuries and underwent surgery.The attack has shocked Poland, where mass shootings are relatively uncommon. Krakow Mayor Lukasz Gibala announced official mourning in the city until Wednesday, while assuring residents and visitors that the city would remain open.You use AI every day. articles.title: Weeks after flydubai incident, 'hostile aircraft' alert triggers panic in Israel
articles.summary: An alert over a suspected hostile aircraft intrusion along Israel's border with Lebanon triggered alarm in northern Israel, before the military clarified
articles.body: An alert over a suspected hostile aircraft intrusion along Israel's border with Lebanon triggered alarm in northern Israel, before the military clarified that it had been caused by a false identification.The alert was sounded over the areas of Zar'it and Shomera. The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) issued a statement shortly afterwards, confirming that the warning was the result of a false identification, The Jerusalem Post reported.The incident comes weeks after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight carrying passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv raised questions over aviation security and the screening of foreign airline crew members.Flydubai incident prompts tighter aviation security checksThe latest alert comes against the backdrop of heightened scrutiny of foreign airline operations following an incident aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073 on September 30.The flight, operating from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia after Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami attacked Indian captain Smit Machchhar and attempted to seize control of the aircraft.Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door despite being injured, allowing passengers, crew members and two off-duty flydubai pilots travelling on the flight to intervene and overpower the co-pilot. The aircraft landed safely in Tabuk.The UAE later honoured Machchhar and the flight crew with the First Class Order of Zayed II for their actions during the incident. The award was conferred by UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.In response to the security concerns, Israel introduced tighter screening requirements for airlines operating flights to and from the country.Under the new rules, carriers must submit crew details at least 48 hours before departure, with subsequent updates required no later than two hours before take-off and a final list at take-off.The measures apply to incoming and outgoing flights operated by both Israeli and foreign airlines and are intended to give authorities more time to conduct background checks.IDF uncovers more than 340 Hezbollah weapons in southern LebanonSeparately, the IDF said on Thursday that its troops had uncovered more than 340 weapons belonging to Hezbollah during operations in the southern Lebanon Security Zone.Soldiers from the 188th Brigade of the 36th Division found the weapons in the Beaufort Ridge and Litani River areas. The recovered material included RPG rockets, anti-tank missiles, mortar shells, firearms, explosives and ammunition, according to the military.The troops also discovered a tunnel shaft approximately seven metres deep inside a civilian home. It contained medical and living equipment.The 188th Brigade began its operations in Lebanon after completing 20 months of active duty in the Gaza Strip and undergoing a training period before its redeployment, the IDF said.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 58-year-old UK father who once won only a dead goldfish as a child has won a mortgage-free £4 million Yorkshire mansion with a lake and £250,000 cash from a £30 Omaze entry, after struggling to build a business
articles.summary: For Malcolm Disson, a childhood fairground disappointment became an unlikely marker of a lifetime spent waiting for a lucky break.
articles.body: For Malcolm Disson, a childhood fairground disappointment became an unlikely marker of a lifetime spent waiting for a lucky break. At 12, he won a goldfish at a fair in Hampstead Heath, only to discover that it was already dead when he opened the bag. More than four decades later, the 58-year-old father has experienced a rather more extraordinary win: a £4 million mansion in Yorkshire, complete with a lake, tennis court and £250,000 in cash, through an Omaze prize draw.As reported by The Yorkshire Post and The Mirror, Disson's winning entry cost just £30 through his Omaze subscription. The prize has made him the owner of a Grade II listed property in Little Ouseburn, North Yorkshire, and marks a dramatic change in fortunes for someone who once struggled to keep his own business afloat.From a dead goldfish to a dream homeDisson's earlier experience of winning was hardly encouraging. The goldfish at the fair remained his most memorable prize for 46 years, until he won £8 on a lottery ticket just two weeks before the Omaze announcement. He had taken the small win as a sign that his luck might finally be changing, but could scarcely have anticipated what would follow.The Yorkshire Post reports that the six-bedroom property comes mortgage-free, with stamp duty and legal fees covered. It also includes furnishings worth £155,000 and a separate two-bedroom cottage, giving the new owner considerable flexibility. According to The Mirror, Disson can choose to live in the house, rent it out or sell it.The estate's lake, tennis court and expansive grounds offer a lifestyle far removed from the homes Disson has occupied over the years. He previously lived in a three-bedroom terraced house in Watford and has spent the past 18 years in Newbury, Berkshire, where he currently owns a semi-detached home.A business built on risk and persistenceBehind the unexpected fortune is a career shaped by a significant financial gamble. In 2004, Disson co-founded The British Shop, a specialist company near Heathrow that handles the packing and international shipping of fine art and antiques.Getting the business started required him to remortgage his home. The first couple of years brought considerable financial pressure, with repayments proving difficult to manage. As reported by The Yorkshire Post and The Mirror, the risk came close to ruining him, but he continued working to establish the company.His professional life has since involved handling valuable collections and arranging their safe transportation for clients with impressive homes. The contrast is now striking: Disson has found himself in possession of a property comparable to the kind of residences he once encountered through his work.A new chapter for the familyThe win is particularly meaningful for Disson's family. He has two daughters, Lilly, 22, and Daisy, 18, and believes the prize will provide them with greater financial security. It has also eased the pressure on him, giving him the possibility of slowing down or retiring earlier, although he has indicated that he remains passionate about his work.His border terrier, T-Bone, will also be part of the family's new surroundings. A keen cook, Disson is already considering bringing everyone together at the Yorkshire property for Christmas.Although he had never visited Yorkshire before seeing his new home, he has since explored York and is looking forward to discovering the area's pubs and local beers. The house also offers opportunities to revisit old interests, including tennis, as well as make time for reading in its library and gardening in its potting shed.A prize with a charitable contributionThe Omaze Million Pound House Draw also generated funds for Blood Cancer UK. The Yorkshire Post reports that the organisation is set to receive £4.5 million through the partnership, adding a charitable dimension to the competition.For Disson, however, the most immediate change is personal: a financial burden has lifted, his daughters have a more secure future, and a first visit to Yorkshire has turned into an entirely unexpected new beginning.Images Courtesy: istock and Mark Field PhotographyYou use AI every day. articles.title: Milwaukee Bucks star Myles Turner has joined a campaign promising 250 pet meals for every point he scores and 1,000 for each three-pointer, following a WNBA player's completed 319,750-meal contribution
articles.summary: A basketball player’s on-court performance could soon translate into thousands of meals for pets of families in need.
articles.body: A basketball player’s on-court performance could soon translate into thousands of meals for pets of families in need. Milwaukee Bucks center Myles Turner has joined an animal welfare campaign linking NBA scoring to support for underserved pet owners across the US. With a new partnership with Humane World for Animals, every point Turner scores during the 2026-2027 regular season will help feed pets, showing how pro athletes can use their athletic platforms to solve problems beyond the game.Basketball points turned to pet foodTurner has signed on as an ambassador for Humane World for Animals’ More Than a Pet campaign, which highlights families that can’t afford to give their pets the care they need, states the report.Turner will be involved in the organization's Points for Pets program as part of the association. For every point scored during the upcoming NBA regular season, 250 meals will be donated to pets in underserved communities. Every 3-pointer will provide 1,000 meals, adds the online report.The campaign will include an online progress tracker on the More Than a Pet website, where supporters can track Turner’s scoring performances and the number of meals those performances translate into throughout the season, also adds the report.That is at a time when access to basic pet care is still a big problem in the United States. According to Humane World for Animals, about 20 million pets live with families living in poverty, and of those animals, around 70 percent have never been to a vet.A personal link to animal welfareTurner’s involvement comes from his own history as a pet owner. In August 2018, his fiancée, Aysia McCloud, adopted their cat Casper from Operation Kindness, an animal shelter in Dallas. The eight-year-old domestic shorthair has since become a fixture in their home.Casper is a lovely boy who is affectionate and sociable. He likes to spend time with the family, have his daily brushing sessions and find sunny spots around the house. His love of squeezing himself into boxes of all shapes and sizes has also become a part of his unique personality.Eventually, the couple’s experience with Casper led to the creation of The Casper Foundation in December 2025. The animal welfare nonprofit primarily works with cats, partnering with shelters, helping with adoption efforts, and creating ways for people to get involved in animal welfare.Following a successful WNBA campaignTurner joins the campaign after a successful previous edition featuring Minnesota Lynx guard Kayla McBride in 2026. She scored 775 points including 126 three-pointers, contributing a total of 319,750 pet meals. Humane World for Animals reported that these meals were then donated and delivered to families across the country.The program kicked off in 2024 with Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball, who scored 1,184 points, which equated to 296,000 meals for pets.Turner’s participation will expose the program to a fresh NBA audience, extending its reach through one of the game’s premier defensive players.Support for families and their petsThe More Than a Pet campaign additionally emphasizes the need to keep pets with the families that love them, rather than letting financial troubles lead owners to give up their companions.Rural Area Veterinary Services, Pets for Life and other programs . Humane World for Animals supports this goal. In total, these programs have assisted more than 750,000 pets in underserved communities. That work involves distributing 38 million pounds of pet food and 12,800 pallets of pet supplies worth more than $130 million.With Turner’s participation, we will raise awareness about the need for accessible pet food, veterinary services and critical resources. This initiative shows how a basketball season can make a difference for a cause bigger than the scoreboard, with every basket an opportunity to help animals and the people who love them.Images Courtesy: istock and Instagram/mylesturnerYou use AI every day. articles.title: COP31 a 'moment of truth': UN chief Guterres urges world leaders to act now on climate change
articles.summary: United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has urged world leaders to take immediate action against climate change, calling the upcoming COP31
articles.body: United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has urged world leaders to take immediate action against climate change, calling the upcoming COP31 summit a "moment of truth" as he prepares to make his final major climate appeal before leaving office at the end of the year.Speaking ahead of the UN climate conference in Turkey, scheduled from November 9 to 20, Guterres said countries could no longer delay action or shift responsibility for tackling global warming to others."This is a moment of truths. We can no longer wait, we can no longer have endless discussions in which everybody tries to push the responsibility to someone else. Everybody must do more, everybody must do more now," he said, according to an interview with the news agency Associated Press.The appeal comes as extreme heatwaves, storms, floods and droughts continue to affect countries amid rising global temperatures. The situation is also being compounded by the El Niño climate pattern, which influences weather systems around the world.For Guterres, whose second and final term as UN secretary-general ends in December, COP31 will be an opportunity to make one last push for stronger international action on climate change.Scientists tell Guterres 1.5-degree target is no longer achievableGuterres recalled that one of the most difficult moments of his tenure came last year, when scientists told him that he could no longer claim the world could still meet the Paris Agreement's central goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.For nine years, he had continued to argue that the target remained achievable if governments took stronger action. However, after consulting scientists ahead of a major climate speech, he was told that the amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases already released into the atmosphere meant the goal was no longer within reach."Scientists told me you cannot say that because that's no longer true," he said."That was an enormous shock for me," he added.The UN is now focused on limiting how far global temperatures rise beyond the 1.5-degree threshold.Guterres said he viewed the failure to meet the target as a failure of political leadership rather than of the world as a whole."But it's not the world that's failed, it's the political leadership that's failed," he said.He argued that tackling climate change required long-term planning and consistent investment, but frequent policy changes in political systems often prevented governments from maintaining that approach.Climate disasters underline urgency of actionThe UN chief also recalled his 2023 visit to the Himalayan region of Nepal, where he warned about the dangers posed by melting glaciers and the risk of glacial lake outbursts, floods and landslides.During that visit, he urged countries to end the fossil fuel era, saying: "The glaciers are retreating, but we cannot."Guterres said that some of the disasters he had warned about occurred sooner than he had expected. Floods in August killed more than 1,400 people, while another 5,600 were reported missing. Scientists said climate change played a role in the disasters.He called for fossil fuel companies to contribute towards supporting countries bearing the worst impacts of climate change, arguing that they should be taxed on their windfall profits."Fossil fuel companies are making huge profits and obviously those windfall profits should be taxed and those taxes should be applied in supporting the countries that are having the more dramatic impacts of climate change," he said.Earlier this month, Guterres also spoke with scientists working on a drifting platform in the Arctic Ocean.He said his interactions with researchers during that visit and his earlier trip to Mount Everest had strengthened his anger towards those who continued to deny or resist necessary climate action.Wars and AI add to climate challengesGuterres said climate change was increasingly intersecting with other global challenges, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran and concerns over artificial intelligence.He pointed to the significant electricity and water consumption and carbon emissions associated with AI."The problem is that all these things are getting combined," he said.He also described the energy shocks linked to wars as evidence of the security risks associated with dependence on fossil fuels.Despite the challenges, Guterres said the global expansion of wind and solar power offered grounds for hope, as renewable energy had become a cheaper alternative to fossil fuels.Guterres says UN has a voice, not real powerFormer US Vice President Al Gore praised Guterres for his sustained efforts to put climate change at the centre of international discussions."António Guterres has consistently been eloquent, forceful and right on target in all of his many statements and initiatives to address the climate crisis," Gore said, adding that he understood it was "the greatest challenge facing humanity".Laurence Tubiana, chief executive of the European Climate Foundation and a key figure in the negotiations that produced the Paris Agreement, said Guterres had pushed climate action further than previous UN secretaries-general.Guterres, however, acknowledged the limitations of his office, noting that countries were not obliged to follow the UN's demands and that major powers had veto authority in the Security Council."Has no real power. We have not much money you know. But there is one thing we have: A voice," he said of the secretary-general's position.With the UN Security Council still deciding on his successor, Guterres said he had three words of advice for the next secretary-general: "Tell the truth."He also urged the public to recognise the scale of the climate threat."Take it seriously because it is an existential threat. And the first thing we need to fight is for our own lives," he said.

articles.title: Beyond marigolds: Rethinking festive florals
articles.summary: The vibrant orange and yellow hues of marigolds have long been synonymous with Indian festivities.
articles.body: The vibrant orange and yellow hues of marigolds have long been synonymous with Indian festivities. But festive floral decor need not be limited to these traditional blooms. From fragrant jasmine and delicate tuberoses to colourful seasonal flowers and lush foliage, there are several ways to bring a fresh perspective to festive home styling. This season, explore a mix of colours, textures and fragrances to create arrangements that move beyond the familiar marigold-laden decor and give your home a distinctive festive touch.A wide array of options to select from There is no end to options that you can explore for festive home decor with regard to nature-themed styling. “Festive floral décor today is becoming much more layered. It is moving towards more interesting combinations of form, texture and foliage. Orchids, anthuriums, chrysanthemums and tuberoses can bring entirely different dimensions to a setting, especially when paired with elements like monstera leaves, trailing amaranthus, delicate ferns or sculptural branches,” says Pawan Gadia, Global CEO and Director at FNP.Beyond conventional flowers, dried flowers, shola flowers and natural materials such as corn husks, dried grass, wheat stems, branches, and corn leaves offer interesting possibilities for festive décor, tells Aditi. M. Agrawal, co-founder of Nestasia. “Such materials bring in texture, earthy tones and a handcrafted quality that works particularly well when building a festive set-up in contemporary Indian homes. The idea is to work with a few distinctive materials rather than rely only on elaborate decorations.”Aarati Neelam, founder & principal designer, Neelera by Aarati Neelam, suggests considering the following flowers and other decorative materials: Tuberoses (Rajnigandha) Jasmine (Mogra)Pink and white lotusesChrysanthemums (Shevanti)RosesCymbidium orchidsFrangipani (Champa)Banana leaves Palm fronds Sculptural stemsFoliage Tactile accents like raw betel nuts, cardamom pods, cinnamon sticks, dried lotus pods, clusters of green limes, pomegranatesBeyond the usual vases and garlandsCreate cascading arrangements: Dress up staircases with cascading florals or experiment with suspended installations at varying heights from chandelier canopies, above bar counters or around mirrors.Rethink the tablescape: Layer flowers and candles into low arrangements, create botanical table runners with banana leaves and foliage, or place floating blooms in glass vessels at varying heights. Add thoughtful details: Tie a sprig of tuberose, eucalyptus or a miniature mogra gajra around linen napkins with raw silk or jute twine for an intimate touch at each place setting. Choose a colour palette: For an understated setting, pair ivory orchids, white anthuriums or tuberoses with sculptural greens, candlelight and brass accents. For a richer festive look, opt for jewel tones such as ruby, wine, fuchsia and plum, complemented by lush foliage. Blush pink and ivory also work well with neutral interiors.Work with your home's existing aesthetic: Take cues from the colours, materials and finishes in your interiors. White flowers and fresh foliage lend a clean look, while deeper reds and burgundy bring warmth. Brass or silver serveware, table mats and decorative platters can add a festive accent.Identify focal points: Instead of decorating every available surface, concentrate on a few areas such as the entrance, dining table or a statement corner in the living room. Balance fuller arrangements with simpler surroundings, varied heights and negative space.Keep the floral palette considered: Avoid combining too many unrelated blooms or statement elements. Choose one or two hero flowers and complement them with structured foliage. Pairing brass accents with dried flowers, for instance, creates an interesting interplay of natural textures and metallic finishes.Be mindful of fragrance: Avoid placing strongly scented candles alongside fragrant flowers such as tuberoses or mogra, particularly near dining areas, as the combination can overwhelm guests. Let the natural fragrance of the flowers take the lead.(As suggested by Aarati Neelam, Pawan Gadia, and Aditi M Agrawal) Ensure the flowers stay freshCondition stems early. Trim stems at a 45-degree angle under running water early in the morning and strip all leaves that would sit below the waterline to prevent bacterial buildupRefresh vase and urli water with cool water (add an ice cube or two an hour before guests arrive) and a pinch of sugar or a drop of mild floral preservativeGently mist arrangements with cool water before the evening gathering beginsKeep fresh arrangements away from direct sources of heat or direct drafts from air conditioners or ceiling fans(As told by Aarati Neelam)One of the most exciting developments in floral styling is treating flowers as part of the space rather than simply as decorative additions. Think sculptural floral installations, low tablescapes that flow across a dining table, or asymmetrical compositions that bring movement to a structured settingYou use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Donovan Atkinson, the 5-year-old who turned cucumbers from his family's garden into a pickle business and sold more than 500 jars from his roadside stand
articles.summary: A roadside stand selling homemade pickles is not the usual sight associated with a five-year-old.
articles.body: A roadside stand selling homemade pickles is not the usual sight associated with a five-year-old. Yet Donovan Atkinson, a young boy from Attleboro, Massachusetts, has found himself running just such a venture, with cucumbers from his family's garden providing the starting point. What began with a surplus of home-grown vegetables eventually developed into a small business, complete with its own name, customers and jars carrying a distinctive label. Known locally as 'The Pickle Kid', Donovan has already sold more than 500 jars since setting up his stand in 2025. His experience has also introduced him to some of the everyday responsibilities involved in selling a product.How Donovan and his mother turned cucumbers into picklesThe idea came about after Donovan's family grew more cucumbers than they could readily use in their garden. Rather than letting the extra produce go to waste, he and his mother, Gabrielle Atkinson, started experimenting with making pickles at home.The kitchen became the first place where the project took shape. Donovan worked alongside his mother, turning the garden harvest into jars of pickled cucumbers. For Donovan, the process offered a way to do something with the vegetables he had helped grow. It also gave the family an idea that could extend beyond their own kitchen.More than 500 jars sold under The Pickle Kid nameIn 2025, Donovan took the next step and opened a roadside pickle stand. The small venture gave him an opportunity to sell the jars to people outside his immediate family and circle of friends.The response was enough to turn the project into a growing local activity. More than 500 jars have since been sold, with customers including neighbours, friends and people who happened to pass by the stand.His business became known as ‘The Pickle Kid’, a name that reflects both his age and the product he sells. The nickname has also become part of the presentation, appearing on the jars themselves.What running a pickle stand is teaching the five-year-oldSelling the jars has given Donovan some early experience with the practical side of running a business. Each sale involves more than handing over a product. He has opportunities to count money, speak with customers and become familiar with the small interactions that come with selling something to the public.His mother has been involved throughout the process, helping him make the pickles and supporting the activity as it developed. At his age, the business remains a family-supported undertaking, but Donovan has already become familiar with several aspects of customer service and basic money management.The experience has also helped him build confidence when dealing with people who visit the stand. These are skills that extend beyond the immediate business, even as the pickle sales remain the main focus.The five-year-old has bigger plans for his pickle ventureThe roadside stand is only the beginning of what Donovan would like to achieve. According to the WCVB report, he hopes to develop The Pickle Kid into a full pickle business in the future. For now, the operation remains centred on the small-scale sales that grew out of his family's garden. There is no indication that the business has moved into wider commercial production, but the more than 500 jars already sold give an idea of how far the original project has travelled. At five, he is still at the beginning of his entrepreneurial experience. But The Pickle Kid already has a name, a roadside stand and a growing customer base.You use AI every day.
